lead.message:
Here is what I understand: Weekend Trips is a small browser app, on desktop and phone, where a group of friends plans a weekend away. It covers who is in, the day plan, and what it costs each person. The repo has no code yet, only documents, and no vision documents are attached. I'm opening round 1 on the experience: two variants of the core screen, so you can react to something concrete instead of answering in the abstract.

Assumptions I made (the draft vision marks them):
- One organizer creates a trip and shares a link. Friends join without accounts.
- Costs are split equally by default, with no payments handled in the app.
- The trip is a single weekend, Friday to Sunday.

I'd suggest the screen domain, since people use this on a screen. The choice is yours in the app.

Round 1 asks the designer for:
1. The trip home screen on desktop and mobile, in two variants: one single page with sections (who's in, day plan, costs), and one with tabs per section. The core loop is "open the link, see who's in, what we're doing, and what I owe".

I'm proposing no tasks yet. Nothing is built until the design is settled and you start building.

Questions are below. Answer what you can, and I'll proceed on my defaults for the rest.

questions.text: Which layout feels closer to how your group would use it?
questions.reason: It sets the structure of every other screen.

steps.name: designer runs asked for by the lead: a short idea

runs.brief:
Design the trip home screen for Weekend Trips, a browser app where a small group of friends plans one weekend away (Fri–Sun). A friend opens a shared link and must see three things at once: who is in (RSVP in/out/maybe), the day plan (timed items per day), and costs (shared expenses, equal split by default, with 'what I owe' prominent). Make two variants: (A) one scrolling page with the three sections stacked and a sticky summary, (B) tabs or segments per section with a summary header. Cover desktop and mobile (mobile-first). Show realistic sample content (a 5-friend cabin trip), the organizer's edit affordances, and an empty first-run state. Keep the feature count small and make the core loop polished. Assumptions: no accounts, link access, one organizer.

The lead asks for: screen; 2 variants side by side, differing in a real choice; for desktop, mobile.

lead.message:
I read the whole app (index.html and style.css, no JavaScript). Today it is one static page, "Trip board", with the line "The weekends we are planning." It shows two hard-coded trip cards in a responsive grid (cards at least 260px wide):

- **Lake weekend**: Sat 17 – Sun 18 Oct, Pine Lake cabin, 4 in (Ana, Jo, Kai, Sam), about $140 each.
- **City walk**: Sat 31 Oct, Old town, 2 in (Ana, Kai) and 3 not yet, about $35 each.

Each card has an "I'm in" button. The button does nothing: there is no script, so nothing is saved or updated. The people, the counts and the costs are plain text. The page has no way to add a trip, no sign-in, and no way to say who you are.

I'm starting round 0, "as it is today". The designer will reproduce the page as it is from the code, on desktop and mobile. You correct it, and later rounds change it.

Here is what I understand so far, and I haven't drafted a vision yet:
- This is a small group of friends planning weekends together (assumption).
- The next version should make planning together easy.

Questions that would shape the vision:

The lead asks for: screen; one take; for desktop, mobile.

verdicts.reasons: The single page and sticky summary use standard browser features and suit the stated small-group scale. No external dependencies or data feeds appear, which supports longevity. However, the shared-link arrival assumes an existing identity, Dev, without showing how a new friend joins. Costs include Maybe participants, contradicting the empty-state promise that everyone In splits equally. RSVP changes recalculate existing debts; removing a payer leaves expenses referring to a missing person. These rules need resolution before construction. About $3.68 remains for building; no measured build estimate or provider-price basis establishes fit within that amount or $10 monthly.

Tabs and the summary header are feasible with standard browser features and suit a small weekend group. The dependency-free approach supports longevity, but the tab experience needs defined keyboard navigation and focus behavior. The shared joining and expense rules have the same unresolved cases as A. Mobile hides the Copy link control, including during organizer setup, although setup requires sharing. No measured build estimate or provider-price basis establishes fit within the remaining approximately $3.68 building budget or $10 monthly.

The single page and sticky summary use standard browser features and suit a small group. The revision adds new-friend joining, returning-friend codes, and separate organizer access. Expense participants are explicit, RSVP changes preserve existing shares, leftover cents have a deterministic allocation, and removed payers retain their financial records. Sample states cover these cases. Mobile Copy link is visible, and the logic reports success only after a successful copy, with a manual fallback. Standard browser features and dependency-free files support longevity. However, code recovery tells friends to ask Maya for a reset without providing that experience; removed friends retain debts but disappear from returning sign-in. Identity persistence and authorization are simulated. About $3.13 remains for building; no measured build estimate or provider-price basis establishes fit within that amount or $10 monthly.

The tabs and summary header are feasible with standard browser features at the stated small-group scale. The revision adds joining, returning identity, separate organizer access, explicit expense participants, preserved historical shares, exact cent allocation, and retained records for removed payers. Mobile Copy link remains available during setup, with conditional success and a manual failure fallback. Tabs now define arrow, Home and End navigation, an associated active panel, and focus retention on tab changes. The dependency-free approach supports longevity. Code reset remains an unsupported recovery promise, and removed friends cannot select their identity to view retained debts. Persistence and authorization are simulated. About $3.13 remains for building; no measured estimate or provider-price basis proves fit within the building or $10 monthly budget.

The single page and sticky summary use standard browser features and suit the small-group vision. The shared prototype now includes organizer code reset, rejection of the old code, successful recovery, and a removed friend's read-only financial view. Production requirements specify persistent sessions, session revocation, code attempt limits, and server-enforced organizer access. Dependency-free browser files support longevity. However, removed friends can request a replacement code, but the organizer's reset controls exclude them. Settlement and the organizer's ability to clear a balance remain undefined. Budget approval remains unsupported: no measured build estimate or monthly price basis exists, and the artifact incorrectly states $3.13 remaining instead of approximately $2.72.

The tabs and summary header use standard browser features and suit the small-group vision. Keyboard tab navigation and focus retention remain specified. The shared prototype adds reset, old-code rejection, successful recovery, and removed-friend financial access. Production requirements now define persistent sessions and server-enforced organizer authorization; the dependency-free approach supports longevity. Removed friends still lack an organizer-accessible reset control, despite having a reset request. Settlement and balance clearing lack defined rules. No measured build estimate or supported monthly cost basis establishes budget fit; the stated $3.13 remainder conflicts with the approximately $2.72 available.
